in_english.name: Burd

Historically, the term 'Burd' has been associated with a type of cloak worn by the Prophet Muhammad. The name carries significant spiritual and cultural importance across Muslim communities worldwide.

data.cultural_impact: In Middle Eastern and North African literature, Burd often appears as a key element in the poetic landscape. For example, in the famous Rubayat of Omar Khayyam, the poet describes reaching the "Burd of Happiness" and the "Burd of Time" in his journey toward self-realization. This concept of Burd as a high point or achievement can be seen in various aspects of Islamic culture, from poetry and literature to architecture and pilgrimage sites.
data.spiritual_significance: In Islamic spirituality, Burd represents a state of divine closeness and submission to the will of Allah. This concept is inspired by verses in the Quran that liken the experience of being in the presence of God to standing on a high place or mount (Al-Anfal: 40 and Al-Mulk: 15). The notion of spiritual elevation and nearness to God through worship, study of the Quran, and acts of charity is a fundamental tenet of Islamic thought and practice, and the term Burd provides a powerful and poetic way to express this idea.

historical_references.context: Burd was the name of a rocky hill near Madinah where the Prophet Muhammad and his companions fought against the Meccan forces during the Battle of Uhud. During the battle, the Muslims' right flank was exposed and the Meccans were able to launch a successful counter-attack. Burd was one of the last strongholds the Muslims held before being pushed back to Madinah. The name 'Burd' is believed to be derived from the Arabic word 'burdah', meaning fortress or castle.

historical_references.reference: Historical records show that Burd Al-Tawil: The Long Bridge of Baghdad, 1259-1260 CE The name Burd carried significant weight in that era.
historical_references.context: Burd Al-Tawil was a bridge built over the Tigris River in Baghdad during the Mongol invasion of the Middle East. The bridge was constructed by the Mongol commander, Hulagu Khan, as part of his siege of the city. The name 'Burd Al-Tawil' means 'long bridge' in Arabic. The bridge was built to provide a means for the Mongol forces to cross the Tigris River and besiege Baghdad from the south. The bridge was also notable for its size and engineering prowess, as it was constructed entirely of wood and was over 1,500 meters long. It remained in use until 1534 CE, when it was destroyed during another conflict.
